questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: All resistances in the circuit in figure are of \(R\) ohms each. The switch is initially open. What happens to the lamp's intensity when the switch is closed?
options: Answer depends on the value of \(R\)
questions.explanation:
Switch Open
The bridge is balanced since \[\frac{R}{R} = \frac{R}{R}\] Hence, no current flows through the central resistor. \[R_{\text{eq, open}} = R\] Switch Closed
When the switch is closed, the top and bottom nodes of the bridge become shorted. \[R_{\text{eq, closed}} = \frac{R}{2} + \frac{R}{2}\] \[R_{\text{eq, closed}} = R\] Therefore, \[R_{\text{eq, open}} = R_{\text{eq, closed}} = R\] Hence, the total circuit resistance does not change when the switch is closed. Therefore, the current through the lamp remains unchanged and so does its power (intensity). \[\boxed{\text{Lamp intensity remains same}}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\text{Remains same}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The impulse response of a network is \(h(t)=1 \text{ for } 0\leq t<1\) and zero otherwise. Sketch the impulse response of two such networks in cascade, neglecting loading effects.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given,
Method 1
\[h(t)= \begin{cases} 1, & 0\le t<1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\] For two identical networks connected in cascade, the overall impulse response is \[h_{eq}(t)=h(t)*h(t).\] \[h_{eq}(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(\tau)\,h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.\] The value of the convolution equals the overlap length of the two rectangular pulses. Hence, \[h_{eq}(t)= \begin{cases} 0, & t<0,\\ t, & 0\le t<1,\\ 2-t, & 1\le t<2,\\ 0, & t\ge2. \end{cases}\]
Method 2
Taking the Laplace transform, \[H(s)=\frac{1-e^{-s}}{s}\] Hence, \[G(s)=H(s)\,H(s) =\left(\frac{1-e^{-s}}{s}\right)^2 =\frac{1}{s^2}+\frac{e^{-2s}}{s^2}-\frac{2e^{-s}}{s^2}\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform, \[g(t)=t\,u(t)+(t-2)u(t-2)-2(t-1)u(t-1)\] Thus, \[g(t)= \begin{cases} 0, & t<0,\\ t, & 0\le t<1,\\ 2-t, & 1\le t<2,\\ 0, & t\ge2. \end{cases}\] This is a triangular waveform of peak value \(1\) at \(t=1\).
Key points
  • The impulse response of cascaded LTI systems is the convolution of the individual impulse responses.
  • Convolution of two unit-height rectangular pulses of width \(1\) results in a triangular pulse.
  • The support of the resulting impulse response is \(0\le t\le2\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the following circuit the \(5\text{ V}\) zener diode requires a minimum current of \(10\text{ mA}\). For obtaining a regulated output of \(5\text{ V}\), the maximum permissible load current \((I_{\text{L}})\) is \(\text{mA}\) and the minimum power rating of zener diode is \(\text{W}\).
questions.explanation: The output voltage is regulated at \[V_o=V_Z=5~\text{V}.\] Hence, the source current through the \(100~\Omega\) resistor is \[I_s = \frac{V_i-V_o}{100} = \frac{10-5}{100} = 50~\text{mA}.\] Applying KCL at node \(A\), \[I_s = I_Z + I_L.\] The maximum load current occurs when the Zener current is at its minimum value required for regulation, \[I_{Z,\min} = 10~\text{mA}.\] Therefore, \[I_{L,\max} = I_s-I_{Z,\min} = 50-10 = 40~\text{mA}.\] The maximum Zener current occurs when the load is disconnected, i.e., \[I_L=0.\] Hence, \[I_{Z,\max} = I_s = 50~\text{mA}.\] The minimum power rating of the Zener diode is \[P_Z = V_ZI_{Z,\max} = 5\times50\times10^{-3} = 0.25~\text{W}.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }40~\text{mA}\text{ and }0.25~\text{W}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An ideal OPAMP is used to make an inverting amplifier. The two input terminals of the OP-AMP are at the same potential because
options: The two input terminals are directly shorted internally
The input impedance of the OPAMP is infinity
The open loop gain of the OPAMP is infinity
questions.explanation:
Virtual Ground Concept:
The output voltage of an op-amp is given by: \[V_0 = A_{\text{OL}} (V_+ - V_-)\] where \(A_{\text{OL}}\) is the open-loop voltage gain. Rearranging the expression for differential input voltage: \[V_+ - V_- = \frac{V_0}{A_{\text{OL}}}\] Derivation & Conclusion:
Since the output voltage \(V_0\) is always bounded between \(+V_{\text{sat}}\) and \(-V_{\text{sat}}\), as \(A_{\text{OL}} \to \infty\): \[V_+ - V_- = 0 \implies V_+ = V_-\] This phenomenon is known as the **virtual ground** (or virtual short) principle, which occurs due to infinite open-loop gain. \[\boxed{\text{(C) The open loop gain of the OPAMP is infinity}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The circuit shown in figure is excited by the input shown in the figure. Sketch the waveform of the output also indicating the salient values. Assume all components to be ideal.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Circuit Operation & Charging Phase:
  • Initially, the capacitor is uncharged so \(V_0 = 0\,\text{V}\).
  • When \(V_i > 0\), diode \(D_1\) conducts (ON) and charges the capacitor following \(V_i\). Thus, \(V_0 = V_i\).
  • Diode \(D_2\) remains OFF as its anode is grounded (\(0\,\text{V}\)) and cathode is at positive voltage \(V_0 > 0\).
  • At \(t = 0.5\,\text{s}\), \(V_i\) reaches its peak of \(1\,\text{V}\), charging the capacitor to \(V_0 = 1\,\text{V}\).
Peak Hold Phase & Final Waveform:
  • For \(t > 0.5\,\text{s}\), \(V_i\) decreases (\(V_i < 1\,\text{V}\)) while \(V_- = V_0 = 1\,\text{V}\).
  • Since \(V_+ < V_-\), the op-amp output switches to \(-V_{\text{sat}}\), reverse-biasing \(D_1\) (OFF).
  • With \(D_1\) OFF, the capacitor has no discharge path and holds its peak voltage of \(1\,\text{V}\) indefinitely.
Key points
  • Precision Peak Detector: The circuit acts as a positive peak detector, tracking \(V_i\) until it peaks and holding the maximum value.
  • Op-Amp Buffer: Eliminates the diode forward voltage drop \(V_\gamma\) inside the feedback loop.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the following circuit (figure), the output \(V\) follows an equation of the form \[\frac{d^2v}{dt^2} + a\frac{dv}{dt} + bv = f(t)\] Find \(a\), \(b\) and \(f(t)\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Integrator Stage Analysis:
For the upper two integrator op-amps: \[V_2 = -\frac{1}{RC} \int V_1 \, dt \implies V_1 = -RC \frac{dV_2}{dt} \quad \text{--- (1)}\] \[V = -\frac{1}{RC} \int V_2 \, dt \implies V_2 = -RC \frac{dV}{dt} \quad \text{--- (2)}\] Substituting (2) into (1): \[V_1 = R^2 C^2 \frac{d^2V}{dt^2} \quad \text{--- (3)}\] Lower Op-Amp Analysis:
At the non-inverting terminal, using superposition: \[V_+ = \frac{1}{2}(V_2 + e^t)\] By virtual short concept, \(V_- = V_+ = \frac{1}{2}(V_2 + e^t)\). Applying KCL at the inverting terminal node: \[C \frac{d}{dt}(V_+ - V_1) = \frac{V_+}{R} \implies RC \frac{d}{dt}(V_+ - V_1) = V_+\] Integrating both sides: \[RC(V_+ - V_1) = \int V_+ \, dt = \frac{1}{2}\int e^t \, dt + \frac{1}{2}\int V_2 \, dt\] Differential Equation Realization:
Substitute \(V_+\) into the integrated expression: \[RC \left[ \frac{V_2 + e^t}{2} - V_1 \right] = \frac{1}{2} e^t + \frac{1}{2} \int V_2 \, dt\] Substituting \(V_2 = -RC \frac{dV}{dt}\), \(V_1 = R^2 C^2 \frac{d^2V}{dt^2}\), and \(\int V_2 \, dt = -RC \, V\): \[RC \left[ \frac{-RC \frac{dV}{dt} + e^t}{2} - R^2 C^2 \frac{d^2V}{dt^2} \right] = \frac{1}{2} e^t - \frac{1}{2} RC \, V\] Dividing both sides by \(-R^3 C^3\): \[\frac{d^2V}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{2RC} \frac{dV}{dt} + \frac{1}{2R^2 C^2} V = \frac{1}{2R^2 C^2} e^t \left(1 + \frac{1}{RC}\right)\] Comparing with \(\frac{d^2v}{dt^2} + a\frac{dv}{dt} + bv = f(t)\): \[a = \frac{1}{2RC}, \quad b = \frac{1}{2R^2 C^2}, \quad f(t) = \frac{e^t}{2R^2 C^2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{RC}\right)\] \[\boxed{a = \frac{1}{2RC}, \; b = \frac{1}{2R^2 C^2}, \; f(t) = \frac{e^t}{2R^2 C^2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{RC}\right)}\]
Key points
  • Op-Amp Integrator: \(V_o = -\frac{1}{RC} \int V_{in} \, dt\).
  • Superposition and KCL: Node analysis combined with virtual ground condition allows modeling active filter systems into standard second-order linear differential equations.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The number of comparators needed in a parallel conversion type 8-bit A/D converter is
questions.explanation:
Given: A parallel conversion (flash) type 8-bit A/D converter. For an \(n\)-bit parallel (flash) ADC, the number of comparators required is: \[C = 2^n - 1\] For \(n = 8\): \[C = 2^8 - 1 = 256 - 1 = \boxed{255}\] (C) 255
Key points
  • An \(n\)-bit flash ADC also requires \(2^n\) resistors and a \(2^n \times n\) priority encoder in addition to \(2^n - 1\) comparators.
  • The flash ADC achieves 1-clock-cycle conversion, making it the fastest, but the hardware grows exponentially with bit-count.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: For what values of `\(a\)' does the system shown in figure have a zero steady state error \([\text{i.e. } \lim_{t \to \infty} E(t) ]\) for a step input?
questions.explanation: The error signal in frequency domain is: \(E(s) = \dfrac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)}\) For a unit step input, \(R(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). Using the Final Value Theorem, the steady-state error is given by: \[\lim_{t \to \infty} E(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sE(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s \cdot \dfrac{1}{s}}{1 + \dfrac{s + 1}{s^2 + 5s + a} \cdot \dfrac{1}{s + 4}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{1}{4a}} = \dfrac{4a}{4a + 1}\] For the steady-state error to be zero: \[\frac{4a}{4a + 1} = 0 \implies 4a = 0 \implies a = 0\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) a=0}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: For what range of \(K\) is the following system (figure) asymptotically stable? Assume \(K \ge 0\)
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation (C.E.) of the given negative feedback system is: \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\) \[1 + \left(\frac{s-5}{s+4}\right)K = 0 \implies s(1+K) + 4 - 5K = 0 \implies s = \frac{5K-4}{1+K}\] For asymptotic stability, the root of the characteristic equation must lie strictly in the left half of the \(s\)-plane : \[\frac{5K-4}{1+K} < 0\] Given that \(K \ge 0\), the denominator \((1+K)\) is always positive. Therefore, the numerator must be negative: \[5K - 4 < 0 \implies K < \frac{4}{5}\] \[\boxed{0 \le K < \frac{4}{5}}\]
Key points
Asymptotic stability means that the system's response decays to zero as time goes to infinity, requiring all poles to have strictly negative real parts.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A unity feedback system has the open loop transfer function \[G(s)=\frac{1}{(s-1)(s+2)(s+3)}\] The Nyquist plot of \(G\) encircles the origin
questions.explanation: The open-loop transfer function is \[G(s)=\frac{1}{(s-1)(s+2)(s+3)}\] The open-loop transfer function has one right-half-plane pole at \(s=1\). Therefore, \[P=1\] Since the system has unity feedback, the characteristic equation will be, \[1+G(s)=0\] For closed-loop stability, \[Z=0\] Using the Nyquist stability criterion (assuming nyquist contour is clockwise), \[N=P-Z=1-0=1\] Thus, the Nyquist plot must make one anti-clockwise encirclement of the origin. \[\boxed{(B)\;\text{Once}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: An electrostatic potential is given by \(\phi = 2x\sqrt{y}\) volts in the rectangular co-ordinate system. The magnitude of the electric field at \(x=1\,\text{m},\; y=1\,\text{m}\) is ,V/m
questions.explanation:
The given electric potential is \[V=2x\sqrt{y}.\] The electric field is obtained from the negative gradient of the potential, \[\vec{E} = -\nabla V.\] Evaluating the partial derivatives, \[\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 2\sqrt{y}, \qquad \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{y}}.\] Hence, \[\vec{E} = -2\sqrt{y}\,\hat{a}_x - \frac{x}{\sqrt{y}}\,\hat{a}_y.\] At the point \((1,1)\), \[\vec{E} = -2\hat{a}_x - \hat{a}_y.\] Therefore, the magnitude of the electric field is \[|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2+(-1)^2} = \sqrt{5}\,\text{V/m}.\] \[|\vec{E}| = 2.236\,\text{V/m}.\] Hence, \[\boxed{2.236}\]
Key points
  • Electric field is the negative gradient of potential: \[\vec{E}=-\nabla V.\]
  • In Cartesian coordinates, \[\nabla V = \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{a}_x + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{a}_y + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{a}_z.\]
  • Magnitude of a vector: \[|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{E_x^2+E_y^2+E_z^2}.\]

An inductor designed with \(400\) turns coil wound on an iron core of \(16\,\text{cm}^2\) cross sectional area and with a cut of an air gap length of \(1\,\text{mm}\). The coil is connected to a \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac supply. Neglect coil resistance, core loss, iron reluctance and leakage inductance. \((\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m})\)

The developed electromagnetic force and/or torque in electro-mechanical energy conversion systems acts in a direction that tends
options: to increase the stored energy at constant \(mmf\)
to decrease the stored energy at constant flux
to decrease the co-energy at constant \(mmf\)
to decrease the stored energy at constant \(mmf\)
questions.explanation:
In electromechanical energy conversion systems, the developed force or torque acts in a direction that minimizes the stored magnetic energy when the flux is held constant. For a magnetic system, \[F=\left(\frac{\partial W_m'}{\partial x}\right)_i\] where \(W_m'\) is the magnetic co-energy. Similarly, \[F=-\left(\frac{\partial W_m}{\partial x}\right)_\lambda\] where \(W_m\) is the stored magnetic energy and \(\lambda\) is the flux linkage. Hence, the force acts in a direction that tends to \[\text{decrease the stored energy at constant flux.}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • At constant flux (or flux linkage), electromagnetic systems move toward minimum stored magnetic energy.
  • At constant current (or \(mmf\)), electromagnetic systems move toward maximum co-energy.
  • Energy and co-energy methods are widely used to derive force and torque expressions in magnetic systems.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse stored energy with co-energy.
  • Remember that the criterion changes depending on whether flux or current (\(mmf\)) is kept constant.
  • Option (D) is incorrect because it refers to constant \(mmf\), whereas decrease in stored energy applies to constant flux.

A Buchholz relay is used for
options: protection of a transformer against all internal faults
protection of a transformer against external faults
protection of a transformer against both internal and external faults
questions.explanation:
A Buchholz relay is used for protection of an oil-immersed transformer against internal faults. It operates due to gas accumulation or sudden oil movement caused by internal faults inside the transformer tank. \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Buchholz relay is used in oil-immersed transformers.
  • It detects internal faults such as winding faults, core faults and insulation failure.
  • It is placed between the transformer tank and conservator.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Buchholz relay does not protect against external faults.
  • It is not used for induction motor protection.

The torque angle of a synchronous machine operating from a constant voltage bus, is usually defined as the space angle between
options: Rotor mmf wave and stator mmf wave
Rotor mmf wave and resultant flux density wave
Stator mmf wave and resultant flux density wave
Stator mmf wave and resultant mmf wave
questions.explanation: The torque angle \(\delta\) of a synchronous machine is defined as the space angle between the rotor magnetic field axis and the stator resultant magnetic field axis. The rotor mmf wave is produced by the DC field winding, whereas the stator mmf wave is produced by the three-phase armature currents. \[T_e \propto F_r F_s \sin\delta\] where \[\delta = \text{space angle between rotor mmf wave and stator mmf wave}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]

Figure depicts the load characteristics of an isolated three-phase alternator, running at constant speed. Match the following sets of operating conditions with the given characteristics. Disregard the effects of saliency, saturation and stator resistance. [figure unavailable]
(a)Constant excitation and non-zero leading power-factor
(b)Constant excitation and zero power-factor, leading
(c)Constant terminal voltage and zero power-factor, leading
(d)Constant terminal voltage and non-zero leading power-factor
questions.explanation:
1. For non-zero leading power factor and constant excitation, armature reaction is partly magnetizing and partly cross-magnetizing. Hence, terminal voltage \(V_{t}\) increases with load current. \[(a) \rightarrow (Q)\]
  2. For zero power factor leading load, armature reaction is completely magnetizing. \[(b) \rightarrow (P)\]
  3. For constant terminal voltage and zero power factor leading current, excitation must be reduced. \[(c) \rightarrow (S)\]
  4. For non-zero leading power factor load, excitation must be reduced initially and increased beyond rated current. \[(d) \rightarrow (R)\]
Therefore, \[\boxed{A}\]

questions.ref: Power System Matrices and Load Flow Q1
questions.explanation:
A voltage-controlled bus is commonly known as a PV bus. At this bus, the generator regulates the terminal voltage while supplying a specified amount of active (real) power to the system. In load flow analysis, buses are classified according to the quantities that are specified and those that must be determined.
Bus TypeSpecified QuantitiesUnknown Quantities
Slack BusVoltage magnitude \((|V|)\), Voltage angle \((\delta)\)\(P,\;Q\)
PV BusReal power \((P)\), Voltage magnitude \((|V|)\)\(Q,\;\delta\)
PQ BusReal power \((P)\), Reactive power \((Q)\)\(|V|,\;\delta\)
For a PV bus, \[P=P_{\text{specified}}\] and \[|V|=|V|_{\text{specified}}\] During the iterative load flow solution (Gauss--Seidel or Newton--Raphson), the reactive power output of the generator and the bus voltage angle are computed. Hence, the quantities specified at a voltage-controlled (PV) bus are: \[\boxed{\text{Voltage magnitude and Real Power}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.question: The inductance of a power transmission line increases with
options: Increase in spacing between the phase conductors
Increase in load current carried by the conductors
questions.explanation:
Concept:
The inductance of a transmission line is determined by the magnetic flux linkage produced by the current flowing through the conductors. It depends primarily on the geometry of the conductor arrangement, particularly the spacing between conductors and the conductor radius. For a three-phase transmission line with symmetrical spacing, the inductance per conductor is \[L = 2\times10^{-7}\ln\left(\frac{\mathrm{GMD}}{\mathrm{GMR}}\right)\; \text{H/m}\] where GMD = Geometric Mean Distance between phase conductors. GMR = Geometric Mean Radius of the conductor. Thus, \[L \propto \ln\left(\frac{\mathrm{GMD}}{\mathrm{GMR}}\right)\] Hence, inductance increases if GMD increases and decreases if GMR increases. Analysis of Options
Option (A): Decrease in line length
Incorrect. The above expression gives the inductance per unit length. Although the total inductance of a line increases with its length, decreasing the line length certainly cannot increase the inductance. Option (B): Increase in diameter of conductor
Incorrect. Increasing the conductor diameter increases the conductor radius and consequently increases the GMR. Since \[L \propto \ln\left(\frac{\mathrm{GMD}}{\mathrm{GMR}}\right),\] an increase in GMR reduces the value of the logarithmic term. Therefore, the inductance decreases. Option (C): Increase in spacing between the phase conductors
Correct. Increasing the spacing between phase conductors increases the Geometric Mean Distance (GMD). As GMD increases, \[\ln\left(\frac{\mathrm{GMD}}{\mathrm{GMR}}\right)\] also increases, thereby increasing the inductance of the transmission line. Option (D): Increase in load current carried by the conductors
Incorrect. Inductance is a physical property determined by the conductor geometry and magnetic medium. It is independent of the magnitude of load current (provided magnetic saturation is absent). Physical Interpretation
When the conductors are moved farther apart, the magnetic flux produced by each conductor links a larger region before interacting with the other phase conductors. This results in greater external flux linkage and therefore higher inductance. Conversely, increasing the conductor diameter increases the internal radius (GMR), reducing the effective flux linkage and hence reducing inductance. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C) Increase in spacing between the phase conductors}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.ref: Distribution Systems, HVDC, Sag and Corona Q1
questions.question: For the same cross-sectional area and conductor material, a distributor requires a larger cross-section than a feeder because the distributor is designed based on
questions.explanation:
Concept:
In a power distribution system, a feeder and a distributor perform different functions. Consequently, their design criteria are also different. Feeder
A feeder carries electrical power from the substation to the distribution area without any intermediate consumer tapping. Since the current remains practically constant throughout its length, \[I = \text{constant}\] Hence, feeders are designed primarily based on: \[\boxed{\text{Current carrying capacity (Ampacity)}}\] Voltage drop is generally not the governing design criterion. Distributor
A distributor supplies power directly to consumers. Loads are connected at various points along the distributor, causing the current to decrease progressively from the sending end towards the far end. Therefore, \[I_1>I_2>I_3>\cdots\] Because consumers are connected throughout the distributor, maintaining the supply voltage within prescribed limits becomes the most important design requirement. The voltage drop is \[\Delta V = IR\] where \[R=\rho\frac{l}{A}\] For a fixed conductor material, - increasing the cross-sectional area \(A\) - decreases resistance - reduces voltage drop - improves voltage regulation. Hence, distributors are designed on the basis of the permissible voltage drop. Analysis of Options
  • (A) Current carrying capacity only
    Incorrect. This is the principal design criterion for feeders, not distributors.
  • (B) Mechanical strength only
    Incorrect. Mechanical strength is important for overhead conductors but does not determine the required electrical cross-section of a distributor.
  • (C) Corona loss limitation
    Incorrect. Corona is significant only in extra-high-voltage transmission lines. It is not a design consideration for distribution conductors.
  • (D) Permissible voltage drop
    Correct. Consumers connected at different points must receive nearly rated voltage. Therefore, distributors are sized mainly to satisfy the allowable voltage-drop limit.
Comparison between Feeder and Distributor
ParameterFeederDistributor
Consumer tappingNoYes
CurrentNearly constantVaries along length
Design criterionCurrent capacityVoltage drop
Voltage regulationLess importantVery important
Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(D) Permissible voltage drop}}\]
Key points
  • A feeder connects the substation to the distribution area.
  • A distributor supplies consumers directly.
  • Feeders are designed based on current carrying capacity.
  • Distributors are designed based on permissible voltage drop.

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.question: A Buchholz relay is used for
options: Protection of a transformer against all internal faults
Protection of a transformer against external faults
Protection of a transformer against both internal and external faults
questions.explanation:
Concept:
A Buchholz relay is a gas-actuated protective relay used exclusively for oil-immersed transformers provided with a conservator tank. It detects faults occurring inside the transformer by sensing the gases generated due to insulation breakdown or abnormal heating. Working Principle:
Whenever an internal fault develops inside a transformer, the intense heat produced decomposes the insulating oil. This decomposition generates gases, predominantly hydrogen, which rise towards the conservator. Depending on the severity of the fault, the Buchholz relay performs one of two functions:
  • Incipient (minor) faults: Gas accumulates inside the relay chamber, lowering the oil level and causing the upper float to operate an alarm circuit.
  • Severe internal faults: A large quantity of gas and oil surge rapidly towards the conservator. The lower float or flap mechanism operates, closing the trip contacts and disconnecting the transformer from the system.
Analysis of Options
  • (A) Protection of a transformer against all internal faults Correct The Buchholz relay detects internal electrical and thermal faults such as:
    • Inter-turn faults
    • Winding-to-earth faults
    • Core heating
    • Insulation failure
    • Localized overheating
  • (B) Protection against external faults
    Incorrect. External faults such as transmission line or bus faults are cleared by overcurrent, differential or distance protection schemes.
  • (C) Protection against both internal and external faults
    Incorrect. Buchholz relay operates only for internal faults occurring within the transformer tank.
  • (D) Protection of induction motors
    Incorrect. Buchholz relays are designed only for oil-filled transformers having a conservator and are not used for induction motor protection.
Applications
Buchholz relays are installed on:
  • Oil-immersed power transformers
  • Distribution transformers with conservators
  • Large generator transformers
They are not used in:
  • Dry-type transformers
  • Hermetically sealed transformers without conservators
  • Reactors
Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(A) Protection of a transformer against all internal faults}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.question:
Match the following:
EquipmentFunction
(a) Circuit breaker(P) Voltage control
(b) Lightning arrester(Q) Power control
(c) Governor(R) Over-voltage protection
(d) Exciter(S) Over-current protection
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
To obtain the correct matching, identify the primary function of each equipment used in a power system. 1. Circuit Breaker
A circuit breaker is an automatically operated switching device used to make or break an electrical circuit under both normal and fault conditions. During faults, protective relays send a trip signal to the circuit breaker, which interrupts the fault current by extinguishing the arc formed between its contacts. Hence, its primary function is: \[\boxed{\text{Over-current Protection (S)}}\] 2. Lightning Arrester
Lightning arresters protect power system equipment from transient over-voltages caused by lightning strokes and switching surges. During normal operation they behave as insulators. Whenever a high surge voltage appears, they provide a low-resistance path to ground, thereby limiting the voltage across the protected equipment. Hence, \[\boxed{\text{Over-voltage Protection (R)}}\] 3. Governor
The governor controls the mechanical input supplied to the prime mover (steam turbine, water turbine or diesel engine). By regulating the mechanical power input, it controls: \[P_m \rightarrow \text{Real Power Output}\] Consequently, governors are responsible for: - Real power control - System frequency regulation - Load sharing among generators Hence, \[\boxed{\text{Power Control (Q)}}\] 4. Exciter
The excitation system supplies DC current to the rotor field winding of a synchronous generator. Changing the excitation changes the internal generated EMF, thereby controlling: - Terminal voltage - Reactive power output Thus, the exciter performs: \[\boxed{\text{Voltage Control (P)}}\] Correct Matching
\[\boxed{\begin{aligned} (a) &\rightarrow (S)\\ (b) &\rightarrow (R)\\ (c) &\rightarrow (Q)\\ (d) &\rightarrow (P) \end{aligned}}\]

questions.question:
Common Data for Questions Q1.07.1 and Q1.07.2
A \(1:1\) pulse transformer (PT) is used to trigger the SCR in the adjacent figure. The SCR is rated at \(1.5\,\text{kV}\), \(250\,\text{A}\) with \(I_L=250\,\text{mA}\), \(I_H=150\,\text{mA}\), \(I_{G\max}=150\,\text{mA}\), and \(I_{G\min}=100\,\text{mA}\). The SCR is connected to an inductive load, where \(L=150\,\text{mH}\) in series with a small resistance and the supply voltage is \(200\,\text{V dc}\). The forward drops of all transistors/diodes and the gate-cathode junction during ON state are \(1.0\,\text{V}\). [figure unavailable]

In the circuit of figure, the switch `S' is closed at \(t=0\) with \(i_{L}(0)=0\) and \(v_{c}(0)=0\). In the steady state \(v_{c}\) equals [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Since the system is initially uncharged, when the switch is turned ON, the diode will turn ON and the current will be given by, \[i = V\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\sin\omega_{0}t\] After \(\omega_{0}t=\pi\), the current reverses, but the thyristor does not allow reverse flow of current. Therefore, the diode turns OFF, and the circuit becomes open. The capacitor voltage is given by \[V_{c} = V\left(1-\cos\omega_{0}t\right)\] When the diode turns OFF, \[\omega_{0}t=\pi\] \[V_{c} = V\left(1-\cos\pi\right) = 2V = 200\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • For an initially uncharged LC circuit, current is sinusoidal during natural oscillation.
  • The diode/thyristor conducts only until current tries to reverse.
  • Maximum capacitor voltage occurs at \(\omega_{0}t=\pi\).
